draft.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander rights
card: After 1945, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and their supporters campaigned against discrimination. Many were denied equal pay, services and a say in the laws that affected them.

In 1965, students led by Charles Perkins travelled through country towns in New South Wales. They exposed and protested against racial discrimination, such as bans from pools and clubs. Media coverage brought the issue to a wide audience.

Australians voted Yes by a very large majority to change the Constitution. The Commonwealth could now make laws for Aboriginal people, and they were to be counted in the census. It did not give land rights.

Campaigns later focused on land. The Gurindji walk-off at Wave Hill in 1966 and the Aboriginal Tent Embassy in 1972 were part of this push, which led to land rights laws and the Mabo decision in 1992.
draft.remember: Protest and votes challenged discrimination first, and land became a major demand as the campaigns grew.

a.q: What was the main result of the 1967 referendum?
opts: The Commonwealth could make laws for Aboriginal people
Aboriginal people were given ownership of traditional land
Aboriginal people won the right to vote for the first time
Discrimination in country towns was made illegal at once
a.why: The referendum changed the Constitution so the Commonwealth could make laws for Aboriginal people, and they were counted in the census. It did not grant land rights, which were won through later campaigns and decisions.
a.clue: It changed who could make laws, not who owned land.

b.q: In 1965, students travelled by bus through towns in New South Wales and protested at a pool that barred Aboriginal children. What did this action mainly achieve?
opts: It drew national attention to everyday racial discrimination
It changed the Constitution to count Aboriginal people
It returned traditional land to the people of the town
It won the Gurindji ownership of their land at Wave Hill
b.why: The Freedom Ride exposed discrimination in country towns, and media coverage made it a national issue. The census change came from the 1967 referendum, and land rights came through later campaigns, so those options describe other events.
b.clue: Think about what media coverage of a protest in a town can do.

a.best: The Commonwealth could make laws for Aboriginal people

b.best: It drew national attention to everyday racial discrimination

proposal.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander rights
card: After 1945, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and their supporters campaigned against discrimination. Many were denied equal pay, services and a say in the laws that affected them.

In 1965, students led by Charles Perkins travelled through country towns in New South Wales. They protested against racial discrimination, such as bans from pools and clubs, and media coverage made it a national issue.

Australians voted Yes by a very large majority to change the Constitution, so the Commonwealth could make laws for Aboriginal people and count them in the census. It did not itself give land, equal pay or the vote, which all Aboriginal people had in federal elections from 1962.

Land campaigns ran alongside the others, such as the Yirrkala bark petitions (1963), the Gurindji walk-off at Wave Hill (1966) and the Tent Embassy (1972). This push led to land rights laws and the Mabo decision in 1992.
